items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in North Dakota
items.meta: North Dakota Bakken royalty owner? Learn how a hyperbolic decline curve actually works before you sell, then get an offer tied to your own well.

sections.html:
If you want to understand how oil wells decline, the Bakken is the textbook, and North Dakota is where the textbook was written.

No American oil play has generated more royalty checks, more confusion about those checks, and more questions about when to sell than the Bakken in western North Dakota. McKenzie, Mountrail, Williams, and Dunn counties saw thousands of horizontal wells drilled between roughly 2008 and today, each one following a remarkably consistent production pattern that shapes what your interest is worth right now.

This page walks through that pattern in plain terms, because understanding it is the single biggest factor in judging whether a buyer's offer on your North Dakota minerals is reasonable.

sections.title: The shape of a Bakken well's life
sections.html:
A Bakken well doesn't produce at a steady rate and then stop. It comes on strong, often at several hundred barrels a day, and loses a large share of that initial rate within the first twelve months. Engineers call this a hyperbolic decline: steep at first, then flattening into a long, shallow tail that can keep producing smaller volumes for twenty years or more.

That shape is why two royalty owners on wells drilled five years apart can see wildly different monthly checks even though both wells are performing exactly as expected. It's not that one well is failing. It's that each well is at a different point on the same curve.

sections.title: Why this matters more in North Dakota than almost anywhere else
sections.html:
Because the Bakken boom concentrated so much drilling into a roughly fifteen-year window, a large share of North Dakota's producing wells are now well past their steepest decline and sitting on that long shallow tail. If your check has been trending down for several years and then leveling off, that's the tail, not a sign the well is running dry tomorrow.

A buyer pricing your interest is essentially forecasting how much oil is left under that remaining curve, discounted back to today's dollars and adjusted for oil price and operating costs. Understanding where your well sits on the curve lets you sanity-check whether an offer reflects that remaining tail fairly.

sections.title: What to check before you get an offer
sections.html:
Pull twenty-four months of check stubs if you can find them. Plot the monthly volume, even roughly, and look at whether the decline from month to month is still steep or has flattened out. A well still dropping sharply month over month is earlier in its life; a well with only small changes has likely reached its long tail.

Also ask whether there's undrilled acreage left in your spacing unit. Many North Dakota units were drilled to full density years ago, meaning there's no realistic new-well upside left, which a buyer factors directly into their price.

sections.title: North Dakota's split-estate and heir realities
sections.html:
A significant share of North Dakota mineral ownership sits with heirs of the original homestead or ranch owners, often split into small fractional interests across siblings, cousins, and estates that were never formally closed. Some of that land is also tied to tribal trust allotments on or near the Fort Berthold Reservation, which carries its own title process through the Bureau of Indian Affairs.

If your interest touches trust land or an unresolved estate, expect the sale process to take longer, since a buyer will need clean title work before closing. That's normal and worth planning for rather than a reason to avoid selling.

sections.title: Selling now versus riding out the tail
sections.html:
Selling converts decades of a slowly declining, unpredictable check into one number today, and shifts the risk of future oil price swings and eventual well abandonment onto the buyer. Holding means continuing to collect whatever the tail produces for as long as the well stays economic, which for many Bakken wells could be another one to two decades.

There's no universally right answer. What matters is that whichever you choose, you're comparing it against an offer that's genuinely tied to your well's position on the decline curve, not a flat number based on the Bakken's reputation.

faqs.q: Why did your North Dakota royalty check drop so much after the first year?
faqs.a: That's expected. Bakken wells lose a large share of their initial production rate within the first twelve months as part of a normal hyperbolic decline, then settle into a much longer, slower tail.

faqs.q: How long will your Bakken well keep producing?
faqs.a: Many wells continue producing smaller volumes for twenty years or more once they reach their long tail, though the exact timeline depends on the specific well, reservoir, and operating costs.

faqs.q: Is your North Dakota interest connected to tribal trust land?
faqs.a: It's possible if your minerals sit on or near the Fort Berthold Reservation. Trust land title work runs through the Bureau of Indian Affairs and typically takes longer to clear for a sale.

faqs.q: Does a lower monthly check mean your well is about to stop producing?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. A well can produce a small, fairly steady volume for many years once it reaches its long decline tail. A steady low check is different from a well approaching its actual economic limit.

faqs.q: What documents does a North Dakota buyer usually ask for?
faqs.a: Recent check stubs, your division order, and the deed or probate documents showing how you acquired the interest, plus the well's API number if you have it.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Montana
items.meta: Own oil royalties in Richland or Roosevelt County, Montana? Learn how Bakken-edge decline curves affect a payout, then get a no-obligation offer.

sections.html:
Montana's slice of the Bakken was drilled earlier than most of the play, which means a lot of Montana royalty owners are further down the decline curve than they realize.

Montana's oil story starts east of Sidney, where Elm Coulee field turned on the modern Bakken boom back in 2000, years before North Dakota's side of the line got crowded with rigs. Richland and Roosevelt counties still carry a meaningful share of that early production, along with newer horizontal wells drilled as operators pushed west and north along the trend. Southeast Montana has a second, smaller story in the Powder River basin, where legacy coalbed methane gas sits alongside a handful of oil tests near the Wyoming line.

If you inherited a fractional interest tied to an Elm Coulee-era well, or a newer unit near Culbertson or Bainville, the math on selling depends heavily on where that specific well sits on its decline curve today, not on what the field was producing a decade ago.

sections.title: Why Montana's Bakken wells are further along than the play average
sections.html:
The Bakken didn't arrive in Montana and North Dakota at the same time. Elm Coulee was one of the first horizontal, multi-stage fracked oil fields in the entire basin, which means many Richland and Roosevelt County wells are fifteen to twenty years into production. A well that far along has almost always rolled off its steep early decline and settled onto a long, low tail of stripper-well output.

That matters for a royalty owner because a check tied to a mature tail well moves slowly from month to month, while the lump-sum value a buyer will quote reflects mostly what's left in that tail, not the big numbers the field made headlines for years ago.

sections.title: Reading a Montana decline curve before you sell
sections.html:
Every Bakken well loses volume fast in its first year or two, then the rate of loss flattens into a long, shallow slide that can run for decades. A buyer pricing your interest is really pricing that remaining shallow slide, adjusted for oil price and how many offset wells might still get drilled around your unit.

Pull twelve to twenty-four months of your check stubs before you talk to anyone. If the monthly volume has been roughly flat or falling only a little, you're looking at tail production, and that changes what a fair offer looks like compared to a well still in its steep early decline.

sections.title: Ownership realities in Richland and Roosevelt counties
sections.html:
A lot of Montana mineral ownership traces back to homestead-era land patents that split into smaller and smaller fractions across generations. It's common to hold a 1/32 or 1/64 interest in a producing unit alongside cousins or an estate you've never fully sorted out, and courthouse records in Sidney or Wolf Point don't always keep those splits current.

Powder River basin owners face a different situation, since a chunk of that acreage is held by coalbed methane gas with only scattered oil interest, and value there tracks gas activity more than any oil decline curve.

sections.title: What a Montana offer typically weighs
sections.html:
A serious buyer will ask for your recent check detail, the API number of the well or wells involved, and whether your tract has any undrilled offset locations left. Interests near the edge of Elm Coulee with no remaining drilling potential price differently than acreage closer to the newer horizontal wells pushing north toward the state line.

Pricing on any given tract varies with oil price, remaining reserves, and how active operators still are in that specific township, so treat any number you hear as a starting point tied to your own decline curve, not a fixed rate for the county.

faqs.q: Is your Montana interest tied to the Bakken or the Powder River basin?
faqs.a: Check the county. Richland, Roosevelt, and parts of McCone and Sheridan sit on the Bakken/Three Forks trend. Powder River, Carter, and Custer counties in the southeast are Powder River basin territory, which leans gas.

faqs.q: Why did your Montana royalty check shrink so much from a few years ago?
faqs.a: Bakken wells decline steeply in their first couple of years, then settle onto a long, shallow tail. If your well was drilled more than five or six years ago, a lower, steadier check is the expected pattern, not a red flag.

faqs.q: Do you need a Montana attorney to sell mineral rights?
faqs.a: It's not required, but if title is unclear, split across heirs, or tied to an old land patent, talk to your attorney or a local title examiner before you sign a conveyance.

faqs.q: How do you find out if your tract has offset drilling potential left?
faqs.a: Ask a buyer directly and request they explain their reasoning, or pull permitting and spacing unit data from the Montana Board of Oil and Gas Conservation's public records.

faqs.q: What documents speed up a Montana sale?
faqs.a: Your most recent division order, twelve to twenty-four months of check stubs, and the deed or probate paperwork showing how you acquired the interest.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Wyoming
items.meta: Wyoming mineral owner in the Powder River or Green River basin? Stacked pay and legacy coalbed gas mean different decline curves. See how each is valued.

sections.html:
Wyoming's Powder River basin has been drilled for coal, coalbed methane, and now stacked horizontal oil zones, sometimes all three under the same piece of ground, which makes ownership here more layered than it first appears.

Campbell and Converse counties anchor Wyoming's modern oil story, where operators have targeted stacked horizontal zones in formations like the Niobrara, Turner, and Sussex within the Powder River basin over the last decade or so. Underneath or alongside that newer development, a lot of the same acreage carries older coalbed methane gas production from the 1990s and 2000s boom, much of which is now well past its peak. Farther southwest, the Green River basin in Sublette and Sweetwater counties holds a mix of deep gas and oil in complex overthrust geology, developed over a longer, more uneven timeline.

Because Wyoming often stacks multiple production eras and formations on the same tract, understanding exactly which zone and which era your specific royalty is tied to matters more here than in a lot of single-formation plays.

sections.title: Powder River basin: newer oil layered over older gas
sections.html:
If your interest is tied to a horizontal well drilled in the last several years targeting the Niobrara or Turner formations, you're likely holding an oil royalty still working through its early decline, potentially with additional undrilled zones left in the same unit since operators have been testing multiple stacked benches across Campbell and Converse counties.

If instead your check traces back to an older coalbed methane well, you're holding a very different asset: gas production from a boom that largely wound down over a decade ago, now sitting on a mature, low tail with limited remaining upside. Your division order will tell you which category applies, and it's worth confirming rather than assuming.

sections.title: Green River basin: deep, complex, and uneven development
sections.html:
Sublette and Sweetwater counties sit atop challenging overthrust geology that's produced both oil and substantial deep gas over several development waves going back decades. Because the geology is more structurally complex than a flat shale play, well performance varies more from tract to tract, and there isn't a single clean decline pattern that applies basin-wide.

For Green River basin interests, your own well's production history carries even more weight than usual in setting value, since basin-wide averages tell you very little about what a specific tract is actually producing.

sections.title: Reading your Wyoming check before you sell
sections.html:
Pull twelve to twenty-four months of statements and note whether the volume is still dropping sharply or has leveled off. A steep, ongoing decline suggests a newer Powder River basin oil well still in its early years. A long, flat, modest volume suggests either mature coalbed gas or a legacy Green River basin well deep into its tail.

Also check whether your unit has multiple formations still available for drilling, since stacked-pay acreage in the Powder River basin can carry meaningfully more upside than a single-zone tract, depending on how active operators remain in that specific township.

sections.title: Wyoming ownership and split estate
sections.html:
A significant amount of Wyoming's subsurface is federal or state minerals leased to operators, mixed with private fee interests, particularly in the Powder River and Green River basins. If your interest is federal minerals, you may receive royalty through a different administrative process than a straightforward private lease, so check your documentation to confirm which applies.

Private fee ownership in Wyoming often traces back to homestead-era patents divided across generations, so if your title is unclear or shared among heirs, talk to your attorney or a title examiner before signing a conveyance, especially on stacked-pay acreage where an accurate legal description affects pricing.

faqs.q: How do you know if your Wyoming interest is oil or coalbed methane gas?
faqs.a: Check your division order, which lists the specific well, formation, and product. Newer Powder River basin horizontal wells targeting the Niobrara or Turner are typically oil; older wells from the 1990s and 2000s boom are often coalbed methane gas.

faqs.q: Why does Wyoming pricing vary so much between wells?
faqs.a: Wyoming's geology, especially in the Green River basin, is more structurally complex than a flat shale play, so individual well performance varies significantly, making basin-wide averages less useful than your own production history.

faqs.q: Is your Wyoming interest federal or private minerals?
faqs.a: It could be either. Wyoming has extensive federal and state mineral leasing mixed with private fee interests. Your lease documentation or division order will indicate which type of ownership applies to your royalty.

faqs.q: Does stacked-pay acreage in the Powder River basin sell for more?
faqs.a: It can, depending on activity, since a unit with multiple undrilled formations may carry more future upside than a single-zone tract, though pricing always ties back to current production and remaining reserves specific to your well.

faqs.q: What documents does a Wyoming buyer typically request?
faqs.a: Your division order, twelve to twenty-four months of check stubs, and the deed or probate paperwork showing how you acquired the interest, plus the well's API number if available.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Colorado
items.meta: DJ Basin Niobrara oil and Piceance gas behave very differently on the decline curve. Learn what determines your Colorado royalty check and how to sell.

sections.html:
Colorado holds two very different mineral stories under one state line: oil-weighted Niobrara horizontals in the DJ Basin, and deep gas in the Piceance Basin on the Western Slope.

If your interest sits in Weld, Adams, or Boulder County, you are in the DJ Basin, and your production is oil-weighted, drilled horizontally into the Niobrara and Codell formations with the same fast early decline that defines every modern shale play. If your interest is on the Western Slope in Garfield, Rio Blanco, or Mesa County, you are almost certainly a Piceance Basin gas owner, a much older and largely conventional or tight-gas play with a different curve entirely.

This page separates the two so you can read your own royalty statement correctly. the buyer cover how a Wattenberg-area DJ Basin oil well declines through its first years, why Piceance gas behaves more like a mature, long-lived asset, and what to weigh before selling either kind of interest.

sections.title: The DJ Basin's Oil-Heavy Decline
sections.html:
Wattenberg field wells drilled into the Niobrara and Codell are horizontal, multi-stage fracked wells, and they behave like the shale-type curve most oil owners eventually learn: a steep drop in production during the first twelve to twenty-four months, often losing more than half their initial rate, followed by a much longer, flatter tail that can keep paying smaller checks for a decade or more.

Weld County has been one of the most actively drilled oil counties in the country for over a decade, so a given royalty interest there may include production from multiple wells drilled at different times, each on its own point along that curve, which is one reason DJ Basin statements can look more layered than a single-well interest elsewhere.

sections.title: Piceance Basin Gas Is a Slower Story
sections.html:
The Piceance Basin, largely in Garfield and Rio Blanco counties, has produced tight gas from the Mesaverde formation for decades, alongside older conventional production. Piceance drilling activity slowed considerably after natural gas prices fell in the 2010s, so most current owners are watching mature wells well past their steepest decline rather than new wells still working through their early years.

Because Piceance gas is largely tied to national gas pricing rather than the more regional dynamics of an oil play, your check there tends to move with broader Henry Hub trends more directly than a DJ Basin oil check moves with WTI.

sections.title: Reading a Colorado Division Order
sections.html:
Colorado's spacing units, particularly in the DJ Basin, are often larger than in older basins, and horizontal wells frequently cross multiple sections, so your interest may be pooled across more acreage than the surface location suggests. Your division order should spell out your decimal interest and which well or wells it is tied to; if you have interests from more than one well, your statement will often show them as separate line items.

Colorado also has some of the more active state-level oil and gas regulatory oversight in the country, including setback rules near homes and schools that have affected the pace of new DJ Basin permitting in recent years, which is worth knowing if you are trying to gauge whether more drilling is likely on your acreage.

sections.title: Timing a Colorado Sale
sections.html:
If your DJ Basin interest is tied to a well still in its first two or three years, you are selling into the steepest, least certain part of the curve, and pricing will reflect that uncertainty. An interest tied to older Wattenberg wells further along their decline, or to mature Piceance gas production, is generally easier to price with confidence because there is more history to work from.

the buyer build Colorado offers from your actual well-level production history, current oil and gas pricing, and county-level activity, and the buyer will tell you plainly which side of the curve your interest sits on before you decide anything.

faqs.q: Is your Colorado interest oil or gas?
faqs.a: Weld, Adams, and Boulder county interests are typically DJ Basin oil, drilled horizontally into the Niobrara and Codell. Garfield, Rio Blanco, and Mesa county interests on the Western Slope are typically Piceance Basin gas.

faqs.q: Why did your DJ Basin oil check drop sharply after the first year?
faqs.a: Horizontal Niobrara and Codell wells follow a shale-type decline curve, often losing more than half their initial production rate within the first twelve to twenty-four months before settling into a longer, flatter tail.

faqs.q: Why does your Piceance gas check track national gas prices so closely?
faqs.a: Piceance production is largely tied to Henry Hub and broader national gas pricing rather than more regional oil dynamics, so your check tends to move with the gas market you read about in the news.

faqs.q: Do Colorado setback rules affect your current royalty?
faqs.a: Setback and permitting rules mainly affect the pace of new drilling rather than production from wells already online. If you are trying to gauge future development on your acreage, current state and county permitting activity is the thing to watch.

faqs.q: What determines an offer on your Colorado interest?
faqs.a: the buyer look at well-level production history, where the well sits on its decline curve, current oil and gas pricing, and county activity levels. A DJ Basin well in its first two years prices differently than one further along its tail, and the buyer walk you through that difference.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Texas
items.meta: Texas mineral owner in the Permian, Eagle Ford, or Barnett? Each region has its own decline curve and value pattern. See how to read yours before you sell.

sections.html:
Texas isn't one oil state, it's five or six different ones stacked under a single set of state lines, and where your minerals sit matters more than the fact that you own Texas minerals at all.

No state spans as much variety in oil and gas geology as Texas. West Texas holds the Permian basin, the most actively drilled oil play in the country, split into the Midland basin on the east side and the Delaware basin to the west. South Texas has the Eagle Ford, an oil and condensate window that's matured considerably since its boom years. North Texas carries the Barnett, mostly a gas play now well into its long decline tail. Northeast Texas touches the Haynesville, another gas-heavy formation. And the Texas Panhandle sits on the western edge of the Anadarko basin, with older conventional production alongside newer activity.

Because these plays are so different in age, product mix, and current activity level, a fair offer on your interest starts with figuring out which of these regions, and honestly which specific county, your minerals actually sit in.

sections.title: Permian basin: the state's most active oil region
sections.html:
Midland, Ector, Reeves, and Loving counties, along with dozens of others across West Texas, sit inside the Permian, where operators continue stacking horizontal wells across multiple formations including the Wolfcamp, Spraberry, and Bone Spring. A lot of Permian acreage still has real drilling upside left, which a buyer factors into an offer alongside your well's current production.

Wells here follow the familiar shale pattern: a strong first year or two, a steep decline, then a longer shallower tail. Where your specific well sits on that curve, combined with whether your unit still has undrilled locations, does more to set your value than the Permian's reputation as a whole.

sections.title: Eagle Ford: a maturing oil and condensate play
sections.html:
The Eagle Ford across counties like Karnes, DeWitt, and La Salle saw its heaviest drilling roughly a decade or more ago, which means a large share of Eagle Ford wells are now further along their decline curve, producing steadier but smaller volumes than during the boom years.

That maturity isn't a downside by itself. It simply means an Eagle Ford offer is priced more around demonstrated tail production and less around speculative future drilling compared to a fresher Permian unit.

sections.title: Barnett and Haynesville: mostly gas, not oil
sections.html:
If your Texas interest sits in the Barnett, around Tarrant, Denton, or Johnson County, or the Haynesville in the northeast corner of the state, you're most likely holding a gas royalty rather than an oil one. Both plays have been producing for well over a decade, and much of that production is now on a long, mature decline tail with limited new drilling.

Value here tracks natural gas markets rather than crude oil, which move on different cycles, so don't assume your Barnett or Haynesville check should follow oil price headlines.

sections.title: Texas Panhandle: layered conventional and newer plays
sections.html:
The Panhandle's Anadarko basin acreage carries decades of conventional oil and gas production layered under some newer horizontal activity. Older vertical wells in this region are typically well into a stable, low-volume tail, while newer wells behave more like other modern shale development with a steeper early decline.

Because both types of wells coexist in the same counties, checking your specific well's spud date and recent production history matters even more here than in the more uniformly-aged Permian or Eagle Ford.

sections.title: Texas ownership realities across regions
sections.html:
Texas mineral title is often split across generations of ranch and farm families, particularly in West and South Texas, where large historic land grants have divided into dozens of small fractional interests over a century. Courthouse records vary widely in how well they're organized county to county, from Midland's active recorder's office to smaller rural counties with thinner staff.

If your title is unclear, shared among heirs, or tied to an old estate that was never fully probated, talk to your attorney or a title examiner before signing any conveyance, particularly on active Permian or Eagle Ford acreage where accurate legal description matters for pricing correctly.

faqs.q: How do you know which Texas play your minerals are in?
faqs.a: Start with the county. West Texas counties like Midland, Reeves, and Loving are Permian. South Texas counties like Karnes and DeWitt are Eagle Ford. North Texas is Barnett, and the Panhandle is Anadarko basin.

faqs.q: Why would Permian basin minerals be worth more than similar Barnett minerals?
faqs.a: Permian wells are more often oil-focused with active ongoing drilling and remaining reserves, while Barnett wells are largely mature gas production with limited new-well upside, which typically prices lower.

faqs.q: Is Eagle Ford production still valuable if the boom years are over?
faqs.a: Yes, mature Eagle Ford wells still produce steady oil and condensate volumes. The value reflects that steadier tail production rather than boom-era output, and pricing varies with the specific well's recent history.

faqs.q: Does Texas have different rules for mineral rights sales by region?
faqs.a: The legal process is the same statewide, but title complexity, drilling activity, and product mix vary significantly by region, which is why an offer should be based on your specific well and county, not a statewide average.

faqs.q: What if your Texas interest is in an area you have never heard of?
faqs.a: Texas has oil and gas activity in dozens of counties beyond the well-known plays. Your division order or a title examiner can confirm the formation and current operator regardless of how well-known the area is.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in New Mexico
items.meta: Own minerals in Lea, Eddy, or San Juan County, New Mexico? Two very different oil stories, two different decline curves. See how each is valued.

sections.html:
New Mexico holds two of the country's most different oil stories side by side, and knowing which one your minerals belong to changes everything about what they're worth.

Lea and Eddy counties sit inside the Delaware basin, the deepest and among the most actively drilled parts of the Permian, where operators are still stacking new horizontal wells across multiple pay zones. Several hundred miles northwest, San Juan County holds a completely different asset: one of the oldest continuously producing basins in the country, where the boom years ended long ago and most wells now sit deep into a slow, mature tail.

Selling minerals in either place starts the same way, by pulling recent check history and figuring out exactly where your specific well sits on its own decline curve, but the conversation from there looks nothing alike.

sections.title: Delaware basin: still early on the curve
sections.html:
Lea and Eddy counties have seen a wave of horizontal development stacked across the Wolfcamp, Bone Spring, and other Delaware basin zones, much of it drilled within the last several years. A well like that is often still working through its steep first-year decline or has only recently rolled onto the shallower part of its curve, which means there's meaningfully more production ahead of it than behind it.

That earlier position on the curve, combined with active offset drilling in a lot of Delaware basin sections, is why interests here tend to price differently than a mature well elsewhere in the state. Depending on activity, a buyer may weigh the possibility of additional wells being drilled on your unit into their offer.

sections.title: San Juan basin: a long, mature tail
sections.html:
San Juan and Rio Arriba counties tell an older story. Much of the basin's oil and coalbed methane production dates back decades, and new drilling has slowed considerably compared to the Delaware basin's pace. Wells here are typically well past any steep decline, producing small, steady volumes that change little from year to year.

That stability has a tradeoff. There's less upside from future drilling to price in, so a San Juan basin offer is built almost entirely around the well's current production and how many years of economic life realistically remain.

sections.title: Reading your own decline curve before you talk to a buyer
sections.html:
Pull twelve to twenty-four months of check stubs regardless of which basin you're in. A steep month-over-month drop points to a young Delaware basin well still working through early decline. A flat or barely-changing volume points to a mature San Juan basin well, or an older Delaware well that's already settled.

Knowing which pattern you're looking at before you get an offer means you can ask informed questions about how a buyer arrived at their number, rather than taking a single figure at face value.

sections.title: New Mexico ownership and title considerations
sections.html:
New Mexico has extensive state and federal trust lands mixed in with private minerals, particularly in Lea and Eddy counties, so it's worth confirming whether your interest is fee minerals or tied to a state or federal lease, since the transfer process differs. San Juan basin ownership often traces back to older ranch and homestead land that's split across multiple heirs.

If your title is unclear or shared among family members, talk to your attorney or a title examiner before signing anything, especially on Delaware basin acreage where an accurate legal description matters for pricing a still-active unit correctly. Ownership disputes and unresolved estates can also slow a closing considerably, so it's worth sorting those out early rather than after an offer is already on the table.

faqs.q: How do you know if you own Delaware basin or San Juan basin minerals?
faqs.a: Location tells you almost everything. Lea and Eddy counties in the southeast are Delaware basin. San Juan and Rio Arriba counties in the northwest are San Juan basin. Your division order will confirm the county.

faqs.q: Why would a Delaware basin offer be higher than a San Juan basin offer for a similar-sized interest?
faqs.a: Delaware basin wells are often earlier in their production life with more remaining reserves and possible offset drilling, while San Juan basin wells are typically mature with less future upside to price in.

faqs.q: Is your New Mexico interest tied to state trust land?
faqs.a: It's possible, since New Mexico has significant state and federal minerals mixed with private tracts, especially in the Permian counties. Your lease or division order will specify the lessor.

faqs.q: Does oil price volatility affect New Mexico offers more than other states?
faqs.a: Delaware basin pricing tends to move more with near-term oil price and drilling activity, while mature San Juan basin interests are more tied to steady production than to price swings.

faqs.q: What paperwork does a New Mexico buyer typically request?
faqs.a: Your division order, twelve to twenty-four months of check stubs, and the deed or probate documents showing how you acquired the interest, along with the well's API number if you have it.

faqs.q: Are royalty rates different between the two basins?
faqs.a: Rates depend on the original lease terms rather than the basin itself, so review your lease alongside your division order to understand exactly what fraction you're owed before comparing offers.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Oklahoma
items.meta: Oklahoma mineral owner in the SCOOP, STACK, or Osage County? Each area has a different production history. See how that shapes a fair royalty offer.

sections.html:
Osage County has been producing oil since before Oklahoma was a state, and that hundred-year head start explains why its minerals are administered differently from anywhere else in the country.

Oklahoma holds several distinct oil stories under one state line. The SCOOP and STACK plays across Grady, Canadian, Kingfisher, and surrounding counties represent modern horizontal drilling, much of it stacking multiple pay zones under the same acreage. The Anadarko basin's older conventional production runs alongside that newer activity in many of the same counties. Arkoma basin territory in the southeast leans gas. And Osage County, wrapping around Tulsa, sits apart from all of it: minerals there are held in a federally supervised trust dating to the Osage Nation's original headright allotments, with production regulated by the Bureau of Indian Affairs rather than the state alone.

Knowing which of these categories your interest falls into is the first real step toward understanding what it's worth, since the ownership structure, the decline pattern, and the market for a sale differ across all four.

sections.title: SCOOP and STACK: newer wells, steeper early decline
sections.html:
Horizontal wells across the SCOOP and STACK have been drilled in significant numbers since roughly the mid-2010s, stacking production from multiple formations like the Woodford, Meramec, and Osage zones under a single unit. Wells like this follow the same pattern seen across most modern shale plays: a strong first year, a steep decline, then a longer, shallower tail.

If your check has dropped noticeably since drilling started but has recently begun to level off, that's typically the well settling into its tail. A buyer's offer on SCOOP or STACK acreage should reflect where your specific well sits in that pattern, along with whether additional zones remain untapped under your unit.

sections.title: Anadarko basin: older conventional production
sections.html:
Beneath and around a lot of the newer SCOOP and STACK acreage sits decades of conventional Anadarko basin production, some going back to the mid-20th century. These older vertical wells are typically well into a long, flat stripper phase, producing modest, fairly stable volumes.

Interests tied purely to legacy conventional wells generally price lower than an active horizontal unit nearby, simply because there's less remaining reserve and less likelihood of new drilling, though value still varies with the specific well's recent production.

sections.title: Osage County: a different ownership system entirely
sections.html:
Osage minerals are held collectively in trust for headright holders, with the Bureau of Indian Affairs overseeing leasing and production under a structure that predates Oklahoma statehood. If you hold an Osage headright or an interest tied to one, the sale and transfer process runs through federal channels rather than a standard county deed transaction, and it typically takes longer.

This isn't a reason to avoid selling if that's the right move for you, but it does mean budgeting more time for the paperwork and working with someone familiar with how Osage transfers actually work, since standard county closing timelines simply don't apply here.

sections.title: Arkoma basin: the gas-leaning southeast
sections.html: Southeastern Oklahoma's Arkoma basin, including counties like Latimer, Pittsburg, and Le Flore, produces primarily natural gas from formations like the Woodford and Fayetteville, with limited oil. If your interest sits in this part of the state, expect your royalty to track gas markets rather than oil, which behaves differently in both price and decline pattern. Much of this production is also older and further along its decline curve than newer SCOOP and STACK wells to the west.

faqs.q: How do you know if your Oklahoma minerals are in the SCOOP, STACK, or older Anadarko production?
faqs.a: Your division order will show the well and formation. Recent horizontal wells drilled since the mid-2010s are typically SCOOP or STACK; older vertical wells producing steadily for decades point to conventional Anadarko basin production.

faqs.q: What's different about selling an Osage County headright interest?
faqs.a: Osage minerals are held in a federal trust structure administered by the Bureau of Indian Affairs, so a sale or transfer involves federal paperwork beyond a standard county deed and generally takes longer to close.

faqs.q: Why is your SCOOP or STACK check declining faster than a neighbor's older well?
faqs.a: Newer horizontal wells decline steeply in their first year or two before flattening out, while older conventional wells nearby may already be on their long, stable tail. Both are normal for their respective well types.

faqs.q: Is Arkoma basin production oil or gas?
faqs.a: Predominantly natural gas. If your interest is in the southeastern counties, check your division order to confirm the product and pricing basis before comparing it to oil-focused areas of the state.

faqs.q: What documents speed up an Oklahoma sale?
faqs.a: Your division order, twelve to twenty-four months of check stubs, the well's API number if available, and any deed or probate paperwork showing how you acquired the interest.

faqs.q: Can you sell just part of your Oklahoma mineral interest?
faqs.a: Often yes. Many owners sell a portion of their interest while retaining the rest, which can make sense if you want some liquidity now while keeping exposure to future production.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Louisiana
items.meta: Louisiana splits between Haynesville gas and oil-weighted plays like the TMS and Gulf Coast legacy fields. See how your specific check behaves and how to sell.

sections.html:
Ask a Louisiana mineral owner what they hold and the honest answer usually depends entirely on which parish you're in. This state runs from pure Haynesville gas in the north to genuine, if complicated, oil production in the south.

The Haynesville Shale across north Louisiana parishes like Caddo, DeSoto, and Red River is one of the largest gas plays in the country, and if that is your interest, you are a gas owner watching a classic steep-then-flat shale decline curve. Moving south and east, the Tuscaloosa Marine Shale straddles the Louisiana-Mississippi line and is a genuinely oil-weighted play, though a difficult one, with high drilling costs and inconsistent activity that has kept it from developing the way Haynesville did. Further south still, Louisiana's Gulf Coast parishes hold decades of legacy conventional oil production, much of it in mature fields that have been producing since well before most current owners were born.

This page separates those stories so you can read your own check correctly, whether it is Haynesville gas, TMS oil, or an old Gulf Coast field, and understand what shapes an offer on each.

sections.title: Haynesville: Gas, Not Oil
sections.html: If your interest is in Caddo, Bossier, DeSoto, or Red River parish, you almost certainly hold a Haynesville gas interest. These horizontal wells follow the typical shale decline pattern: a fast drop in the first year or two, often losing more than half the initial rate, followed by a long tail. Haynesville drilling activity has moved in cycles tied closely to gas prices and, more recently, to LNG export demand along the Gulf Coast, so your check can move with national gas-market news more than with anything happening on your specific lease.

sections.title: The Tuscaloosa Marine Shale's Oil Promise and Its Limits
sections.html:
The TMS, running through parishes like East Feliciana, St. Helena, and Tangipahoa before crossing into Mississippi, holds oil, and operators have periodically tried to develop it aggressively, but the play has faced real technical challenges: high drilling costs, a corrosive, high-pressure formation, and gas-oil ratios that complicate economics. Activity has stalled and restarted more than once over the past decade.

If your interest is in the TMS, honesty matters here: this is a play with real oil in the ground but an inconsistent drilling history, so an owner's check depends heavily on whether an operator is currently active on or near your acreage rather than on the play's overall promise.

sections.title: Gulf Coast Legacy Fields
sections.html:
South Louisiana's Gulf Coast parishes, including areas around Lafayette, Houma, and the coastal wetlands, sit on some of the oldest conventional oil production in the country, dating back to the early twentieth century. Many of these fields are well past their peak and producing on long, shallow declines, sometimes from wells that have been reworked and re-completed multiple times over the decades.

Louisiana's coastal geography also brings its own complications, including access, environmental permitting, and in some cases state coastal-zone rules that affect operator activity, which is worth knowing if you are trying to gauge whether more drilling is likely near your interest.

sections.title: Selling Across Louisiana's Different Plays
sections.html:
Because Louisiana holds such different production types under one state line, the buyer price interests using the specifics of your own parish and well, not a statewide average. A Haynesville well two years into its decline prices very differently than a mature Gulf Coast stripper well or a TMS interest with uncertain future drilling.

the buyer pull your recent royalty history, check current activity levels in your parish, and weigh current oil or gas pricing depending on your resource before putting together an offer, and the buyer will tell you plainly which category your interest falls into.

faqs.q: Is Haynesville an oil play or a gas play?
faqs.a: Gas. Haynesville wells in Caddo, Bossier, DeSoto, and Red River parishes produce natural gas, and their checks move with national gas pricing and LNG export demand more than with oil markets.

faqs.q: Is the Tuscaloosa Marine Shale a good oil play?
faqs.a: It holds real oil, but drilling activity has been inconsistent due to high costs and a difficult formation. Whether your specific interest is generating income depends heavily on whether an operator is currently active nearby more than on the play's overall geology.

faqs.q: Why is your south Louisiana oil check so steady?
faqs.a: Many Gulf Coast fields have been producing for close to a century and are well past their steepest decline, so volume changes slowly and your check moves mostly with oil price.

faqs.q: Do Louisiana coastal rules affect your mineral interest?
faqs.a: They can affect the pace of new drilling and access in coastal-zone areas. Existing production continues under current permits, but coastal environmental and access rules are worth understanding if you are trying to gauge future activity.

faqs.q: What determines an offer on your Louisiana interest?
faqs.a: It depends heavily on which play you're in. the buyer look at your recent royalty history, current parish-level drilling activity, and oil or gas pricing specific to your resource, and explain which category your interest falls into before quoting a figure.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Arkansas
items.meta: Own an Arkansas royalty tied to old El Dorado oil or the Smackover trend? Learn how the check behaves and what determines a fair offer, no obligation.

sections.html:
Arkansas's oil story starts a century ago in El Dorado, and a surprising number of royalty checks in south Arkansas still trace back to that original Smackover boom.

When people mention Arkansas oil and gas today, the Fayetteville Shale in the north-central part of the state usually comes up first, but Fayetteville wells produce gas, not oil. The state's real oil legacy sits further south, in Union, Ouachita, and Columbia counties, where the 1921 El Dorado discovery kicked off one of the fastest oil booms in American history and left behind a dense patchwork of small, long-lived wells still paying royalties today.

If your check comes from a county along that southern Smackover trend, this page explains how a check from a decades-old Arkansas oil well behaves differently than one from a young shale play, what the ownership picture typically looks like after a century of inherited interests, and how the newer Smackover lithium brine interest in the same trend fits into the picture without changing your oil royalty itself.

sections.title: El Dorado's Long Tail
sections.html:
The El Dorado field and the broader Smackover trend across south Arkansas were producing oil before most current owners' grandparents were born. A well that came in during the 1920s or 1930s and is still on production today has long since passed through its steepest decline and settled into a slow, shallow slide, often propped up by decades of waterflooding and workovers that kept marginal volumes flowing.

That history matters for what to expect from your check. A century-old stripper well is not going to swing wildly month to month the way a new horizontal well does in its first two years. Instead, your statement moves mostly with the price of oil and with whatever small mechanical or workover changes the operator makes on that particular lease.

sections.title: Fayetteville Gas Is a Different Animal
sections.html:
If your interest sits in Van Buren, Cleburne, Conway, or one of the other core Fayetteville Shale counties, you are a gas owner, and the play's decline curve looks like most shale gas plays: a sharp initial drop in the first one to three years followed by a long, flatter tail. Fayetteville drilling activity slowed considerably after its mid-2010s peak, so most owners in this play today are watching mature, declining production rather than new wells coming online.

It is worth knowing which category you fall into before you compare notes with a neighbor or a relative, since a Fayetteville gas check and a Smackover oil check respond to completely different price signals and completely different points on their respective curves.

sections.title: What the Lithium Brine News Means for Oil Owners
sections.html:
South Arkansas has drawn recent attention for lithium recovery from the same Smackover brine that has produced oil for a century. That is a genuinely different resource and a different set of leases, and most existing oil and gas royalty owners will not automatically see lithium income unless their deed or a new agreement specifically covers brine minerals. It does not change what your existing oil royalty check is worth, though it has raised general interest in the region.

If you have questions about whether your specific mineral deed language extends to brine or lithium, that is a title question worth running past an attorney rather than assuming either way.

sections.title: Selling an Interest With a Long Production History
sections.html:
A well with eighty or ninety years of production history is, in one sense, easier to price than a brand-new well, because there is decades of real data showing how it behaves rather than a projection. the buyer build offers on southern Arkansas interests from that documented history, current oil pricing, and how much productive life the operator's own reports suggest remains.

For Fayetteville gas interests, the buyer look at where the well sits on its shale decline curve and current gas pricing, since a well several years past its peak is valued differently than one still working through its early drop.

faqs.q: Is Arkansas an oil state or a gas state?
faqs.a: Both, depending on where your interest is. South Arkansas counties like Union, Ouachita, and Columbia along the Smackover trend are legacy oil country dating to the 1921 El Dorado boom. North-central counties over the Fayetteville Shale are gas.

faqs.q: Why does your south Arkansas oil check barely move month to month?
faqs.a: Many south Arkansas wells have been producing since the 1920s or 1930s and are now on the long, flat tail of their decline curve, often under waterflood. Oil price, not a changing production volume, drives most of the movement you will see.

faqs.q: Does the Smackover lithium boom affect your oil royalty?
faqs.a: Not automatically. Lithium is recovered from the same brine formation but under separate leases and deed language. Your existing oil royalty is unaffected unless your specific mineral deed covers brine minerals, which is worth confirming with an attorney if you are unsure.

faqs.q: How old are most Arkansas oil royalty interests?
faqs.a: Many in the Smackover trend trace back nearly a century to the original El Dorado-era leases, which means ownership has often split across three or more generations of heirs by now.

faqs.q: What determines an offer on your Arkansas interest?
faqs.a: For Smackover oil interests, the buyer look at the well's long production history and current oil pricing. For Fayetteville gas interests, the buyer look at the well's position on its shale decline curve and current gas pricing. Either way, the number is tied to your actual data, not a flat promise.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Kansas
items.meta: Kansas splits between Mississippian Lime oil and Hugoton gas. Learn how water cut affects an oil check here and what it takes to get a fair offer.

sections.html:
Kansas oil owners in the Mississippian Lime deal with something most other plays do not talk about enough: water. Lots of it, and it changes how the check behaves.

South-central Kansas, across counties like Barber, Harper, Comanche, and Kingman, sits on the Mississippian Lime, an oil-weighted play that saw heavy horizontal drilling activity in the early 2010s. Southwest Kansas, by contrast, sits over the Hugoton field, one of the largest natural gas fields ever discovered in North America, spanning into Oklahoma and Texas. If your interest is Hugoton, you are a gas owner; if it is Mississippian Lime, you are an oil owner, and this page focuses on what that oil production actually looks like.

The defining feature of Mississippian Lime oil wells is high water cut, meaning these wells produce a lot of saltwater alongside the oil. That reality shapes lifting costs, operator economics, and ultimately how your royalty check behaves over time, so it is worth understanding before you think about selling.

sections.title: Why Water Cut Matters for Your Kansas Check
sections.html:
A typical Mississippian Lime well produces several barrels of saltwater for every barrel of oil, and the operator has to gather, transport, and dispose of that water, usually through injection wells, at real cost. When oil prices are strong, that cost is easy to absorb; when prices fall, high-water-cut wells are often among the first an operator slows down or shuts in, because the economics get thin faster than on a lower-water-cut well elsewhere.

This means your Mississippian Lime royalty check can be more sensitive to oil price swings than a comparable well in a play with lower water cut, and it is worth watching your statement's oil volume alongside price rather than assuming price alone explains every change.

sections.title: The 2010s Drilling Wave and What Came After
sections.html:
The Mississippian Lime saw a real horizontal drilling boom roughly from 2011 to 2015, with a large number of wells drilled across Barber, Harper, and neighboring counties. Activity slowed considerably after oil prices fell in 2014 and 2015, and it has stayed relatively quiet since, so most current owners are watching wells that are now several years to a decade past their initial completion, sitting on the flatter, later part of the decline curve rather than early volatile production.

That timing matters for how you read your own history. If your check has been fairly steady over the past several years, with change tied mostly to price rather than a falling volume line, that is a sign your well has already moved into the mature phase of production, which is generally easier to value than a well still working through its first two or three years.

sections.title: Hugoton Gas: A Different Kansas Story Entirely
sections.html: If your interest is in Grant, Stevens, Haskell, or a neighboring far-southwest Kansas county, you are almost certainly a Hugoton gas owner. Hugoton has been producing since the 1920s and is one of the longest-lived gas fields in the country, with a slow, gradual decline shaped more by field-wide depletion over a century than by any single well's curve. Your check there moves largely with national gas pricing.

sections.title: Selling a Mississippian Lime Interest
sections.html:
Because Mississippian Lime wells are now years removed from their initial drilling wave, the buyer can price them from real, multi-year production history rather than a projection, which generally makes for a more confident offer. the buyer weigh your recent water and oil volumes together, current oil pricing, and county-level activity when building a figure.

For Hugoton gas interests, the buyer look at the field's long-term depletion trend and current gas pricing instead, since the underlying dynamics are so different from an oil-weighted Mississippian Lime interest.

faqs.q: Is Kansas an oil state or a gas state?
faqs.a: Both. South-central counties like Barber, Harper, and Comanche are Mississippian Lime oil country. Far-southwest counties like Grant, Stevens, and Haskell sit over the Hugoton gas field.

faqs.q: Why does your Mississippian Lime check swing more than you expected?
faqs.a: These wells typically produce a high ratio of saltwater to oil, and disposal costs eat into the economics faster when oil prices drop. That makes the checks more sensitive to price swings than a comparable well with lower water cut.

faqs.q: Is Mississippian Lime drilling still active?
faqs.a: Not at the pace it was during the 2011 to 2015 boom. Activity slowed considerably after the 2014 to 2015 oil price drop, and most current wells are several years to a decade past their initial completion.

faqs.q: How old is Hugoton field production?
faqs.a: Hugoton has been producing since the 1920s, making it one of the longest-lived gas fields in the country. Its decline is gradual and field-wide rather than tied to any single well's curve.

faqs.q: What determines an offer on your Kansas interest?
faqs.a: For Mississippian Lime oil, the buyer weigh your recent oil and water volumes together, current oil pricing, and county activity. For Hugoton gas, the buyer weigh the field's long-term depletion trend and current gas pricing. Either way, the figure is grounded in your actual data.

faqs.q: Should you expect much new drilling near your Mississippian Lime interest?
faqs.a: Activity has stayed relatively light since the mid-2010s slowdown, so a near-term jump in drilling near an established interest is not the typical case. Most current value comes from the well's existing production history rather than expected new wells.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Pennsylvania
items.meta: Pennsylvania mineral owner? The Marcellus is a gas play, not oil. Learn how gas royalties actually get valued here before you consider a sale.

sections.html:
Let's be straightforward about it: Pennsylvania is a natural gas state, not an oil state, and any conversation about your minerals should start from that fact.

Pennsylvania's modern mineral wealth comes almost entirely from the Marcellus shale, one of the largest natural gas fields in the world, running through counties like Washington, Greene, Susquehanna, and Bradford. Deeper Utica shale gas adds a second layer in parts of the state. There's a small historical footnote worth knowing: the world's first commercial oil well was drilled near Titusville in 1859, and pockets of very old, shallow oil production still exist in northwestern counties like Venango and McKean, but that's a tiny fraction of what Pennsylvania minerals are worth today compared to Marcellus gas.

If you're holding a Pennsylvania interest and wondering whether to sell, the real question is almost always about a gas royalty's decline pattern and pricing, not an oil decline curve, so this page focuses on getting that part right.

sections.title: How a Marcellus gas well declines
sections.html:
Marcellus wells behave similarly to other modern shale wells in one respect: they produce heavily in the first year or two, then decline into a longer, shallower tail that can run for many years. What's different from an oil well is that your royalty check moves with natural gas prices, which have their own seasonal and macro patterns separate from crude oil markets.

If your check has dropped since the well was first turned online, that's expected behavior for a maturing gas well, not necessarily a warning sign. Pulling recent check history is still the best way to understand where your specific well sits before evaluating any offer.

sections.title: The small legacy oil pocket in northwestern Pennsylvania
sections.html:
Venango, McKean, Warren, and a handful of nearby counties still hold scattered shallow oil wells dating back over a century, remnants of the original American oil boom. These wells are typically stripper production now, small and steady, operated at a scale far removed from the Marcellus's modern industrial pace.

If your interest is one of these legacy oil tracts, don't expect it to price like a modern shale well. It will be valued on its own modest, long-running production history, which is a fundamentally different asset than a Marcellus gas royalty even though both are technically mineral interests in Pennsylvania.

sections.title: Pennsylvania ownership and lease terms
sections.html:
Pennsylvania has a long history of severed mineral estates going back to 19th-century land transactions, meaning a lot of surface owners today don't own the minerals beneath their own land, and vice versa. Lease terms, royalty rates, and post-production cost deductions vary widely depending on when your lease was signed, with older leases sometimes carrying less favorable terms than more recent ones.

Before selling, review your lease and division order carefully, or have your attorney do so, since the specific deductions and royalty fraction written into an old Pennsylvania lease directly affect what a buyer will offer for the remaining interest.

sections.title: What a Pennsylvania gas offer typically weighs
sections.html:
A buyer evaluating your Marcellus interest will ask for recent check stubs, your division order, and details on whether your unit sits in an active drilling area or one where development has largely wound down. Counties like Washington and Greene have seen more continuous activity than some of the more rural northern tier counties, which can affect how much remaining upside a buyer is willing to price in.

Post-production costs, meaning the deductions taken for gathering, compression, and transportation before your royalty is calculated, can vary meaningfully between leases and directly affect your net check, so understanding your specific deduction structure helps you judge whether an offer reflects your true production accurately.

faqs.q: Is Pennsylvania an oil state or a gas state?
faqs.a: Overwhelmingly gas today. The Marcellus and deeper Utica shale produce natural gas across most of the state. A small amount of legacy oil production remains in northwestern counties, but it's a minor share of overall value.

faqs.q: Why did your Pennsylvania royalty check drop after the first couple of years?
faqs.a: Marcellus gas wells decline steeply in their early years before settling into a longer, shallower tail, similar to shale oil wells elsewhere. A declining then leveling check is typical, not unusual.

faqs.q: Does your old Pennsylvania lease affect what you would get for selling?
faqs.a: Yes. Royalty rate and post-production cost deductions vary by lease vintage, and both directly affect the net value of your interest. Review your lease terms, or have your attorney review them, before comparing offers.

faqs.q: Do you own the minerals under your own land in Pennsylvania?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Pennsylvania has a long history of severed mineral estates, so it's common for surface and mineral ownership to belong to different parties. Your deed history will clarify this.

faqs.q: What are post-production cost deductions?
faqs.a: Charges for gathering, compressing, and transporting gas before it reaches market, deducted from your royalty under many Pennsylvania leases. The exact deduction structure varies by lease and affects your net check.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in West Virginia
items.meta: West Virginia mineral owner? From Burning Springs' 1860s oil boom to today's Marcellus gas wells, learn how your specific interest gets valued before selling.

sections.html:
West Virginia had one of the country's first oil booms in the 1860s along the Kanawha River, and it's now home to some of the largest natural gas wells ever drilled, which tells you how much this state's mineral history spans.

Burning Springs, in Wirt County, was the site of an oil boom during the Civil War era, one of America's earliest, and scattered shallow legacy oil wells from that century-and-a-half-old history still exist across central and southern West Virginia. That history is a small footnote next to what dominates the state's mineral value today: the Marcellus and deeper Utica shale running through the northern panhandle and north-central counties like Wetzel, Marshall, and Doddridge, where operators have drilled some of the longest lateral gas wells in the country.

If you own West Virginia minerals, figuring out whether your interest is tied to modern Marcellus or Utica gas versus a legacy conventional well changes what a fair value conversation looks like.

sections.title: Marcellus and Utica: the modern engine
sections.html:
Wetzel, Marshall, Doddridge, and Tyler counties sit at the heart of West Virginia's modern shale development, where wells routinely run laterals two or three miles long to maximize gas recovery per pad. These wells decline steeply in their first year or two before flattening into a long production tail, similar to shale wells anywhere else, just with gas instead of oil as the product.

Because a meaningful share of this development happened more recently than in neighboring Pennsylvania, some West Virginia units still carry undrilled potential, which a buyer factors into an offer alongside your well's current production trend.

sections.title: Legacy conventional wells across central and southern counties
sections.html:
Away from the Marcellus core, especially in central and southern counties with roots in West Virginia's older oil and gas history, a lot of production comes from shallow, conventional wells drilled decades ago. These wells are typically far past any steep decline, producing small, steady volumes that have held roughly flat for years.

Interests tied to this older production price differently than active Marcellus acreage, built mostly around demonstrated stripper-well output rather than any expectation of new drilling.

sections.title: West Virginia's severed mineral estate history
sections.html:
West Virginia has one of the longest histories of severed mineral ownership in the country, with many mineral estates split from the surface more than a century ago through old timber and coal-era transactions. It's common for a current landowner to have no mineral rights at all, and equally common for a mineral owner to live far from the tract, sometimes having inherited an interest they didn't know existed.

Given how old some of these severances are, title research can take real time, particularly tracing chain of title back through 19th and early 20th century deeds. A local title examiner or your attorney can confirm exactly what you hold before you consider an offer.

sections.title: Reading your own production history before selling
sections.html:
Whether you're sitting on modern Marcellus gas or a legacy conventional well, twelve to twenty-four months of check stubs tell you far more than the state's reputation does. A steep recent decline points to newer development still working through its early years; a flat, low volume points to mature or legacy production.

That history, combined with clean title, is what actually drives a fair offer, so gather it before you start comparing numbers from different buyers.

faqs.q: Is your West Virginia interest gas or legacy oil?
faqs.a: Check your division order. Modern Marcellus and Utica production in the northern and north-central counties is predominantly natural gas. Older conventional wells in central and southern counties may include legacy oil production.

faqs.q: Why is West Virginia mineral title often complicated?
faqs.a: The state has a long history of severed mineral estates dating back over a century to old timber and coal transactions, which means title research often has to trace chain of ownership through many decades of deeds.

faqs.q: Do you own the minerals under land you don't personally own the surface of?
faqs.a: It's possible and common in West Virginia. Surface and mineral ownership are frequently split, sometimes for generations, so your deed history is the only reliable way to confirm what you actually hold.

faqs.q: Why do some West Virginia gas wells have such long laterals?
faqs.a: Operators in the Marcellus and Utica have pushed lateral lengths further here than in many other shale plays to maximize recovery per well pad, which can affect both production volume and decline pattern.

faqs.q: What paperwork does a West Virginia buyer typically request?
faqs.a: Your division order, recent check stubs, and the deed or probate documents showing how you acquired the interest. Older or severed estates may require additional title research before closing.

faqs.q: Is legacy oil production in West Virginia still worth anything?
faqs.a: Yes, though modestly. Shallow conventional wells from the state's older oil history can still produce small, steady volumes worth pricing fairly, even without the scale of modern Marcellus development.

faqs.q: Can you sell only part of your West Virginia interest?
faqs.a: Often yes. Many owners sell a portion of an interest while retaining the rest, which can make sense when weighing current value against ongoing production from an active well.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Ohio
items.meta: Ohio Utica shale mineral owner? Most of eastern Ohio's Utica is gas and NGLs, not oil. Learn what that means for value before you sell your interest.

sections.html:
Before anything else, an honest starting point: most of eastern Ohio's Utica production is gas and natural gas liquids, and a smaller slice is oil, so knowing which you actually own changes the whole conversation.

The Utica shale runs under a wide swath of eastern Ohio, but the rock doesn't produce the same thing everywhere. Belmont, Monroe, and Noble counties sit deep in the wet gas and condensate window, where wells produce mostly natural gas with valuable liquids mixed in. Guernsey, Harrison, and parts of Carroll County lean drier still. Genuine oil production is limited to a narrower band, so if your division order shows an oil royalty, you're in a smaller category of Ohio mineral owner than most.

Whichever product your well makes, the sale process starts the same way: pulling your recent check stubs and figuring out where that specific well sits in its production life before you weigh an offer.

sections.title: Wet gas, dry gas, and where oil actually shows up
sections.html:
The Utica's composition shifts depending on depth and location within the play. Closer to the basin's deeper, hotter areas, wells tend to produce dry gas with little liquid content. Move toward the shallower edges, and wells produce more condensate and natural gas liquids, with true crude oil showing up mainly in a limited stretch of counties along the play's western fringe.

This matters directly for royalty value, because gas, NGLs, and oil are priced differently and respond to different market cycles. A check built mostly on NGL revenue behaves differently month to month than one built on crude, so don't assume your Utica royalty tracks national oil headlines just because it's an oil and gas lease. Reviewing your division order line by line is the most reliable way to see exactly what mix of products your specific well is producing.

sections.title: Reading your Ohio decline curve
sections.html:
Utica wells, like most modern horizontal shale wells, decline quickly in their first year or two before settling into a longer, shallower tail. If your well was drilled during the play's main development years, roughly the early-to-mid 2010s through the present, you're likely looking at a well somewhere between that early decline and the flatter tail, depending on exact spud date. Wells drilled closer to the play's early boom years are more likely to already be well into that flatter, more predictable stage.

Twelve to twenty-four months of check history will tell you which phase you're in far more reliably than guessing from memory. A buyer's offer should reflect that specific position, not a general assumption about the Utica as a whole.

sections.title: Ohio ownership and the split-estate reality
sections.html:
Eastern Ohio has a long history of family farmland passed down across generations, and it's common for mineral interests to be split among numerous heirs, sometimes without formal probate ever clearing up who owns what fraction. County recorder offices in places like St. Clairsville and Cambridge hold decades of these records, and gaps are common.

If your title isn't clean, or you're one of several cousins holding a small piece of a larger family tract, talk to your attorney or a title examiner before signing a conveyance, since unclear title can slow or complicate a sale. Sorting out an unresolved estate before you start comparing offers usually saves time later in the process.

faqs.q: Is your Ohio Utica interest oil or gas?
faqs.a: Most of eastern Ohio's Utica production is gas or gas with natural gas liquids, not crude oil. Check your division order or check stub, which will list the specific product and pricing basis.

faqs.q: Why does your Ohio royalty check fluctuate so much?
faqs.a: If your production includes natural gas liquids, the check reflects a mix of commodity prices that can move independently of both oil and dry gas prices, which creates more month-to-month variation.

faqs.q: How do you find out which part of the Utica window your well is in?
faqs.a: Your division order or the operator's well records will show the product mix. Wells producing more oil and condensate sit toward the play's western, shallower edge.

faqs.q: Is title on your Ohio interest likely to be complicated?
faqs.a: It's common in eastern Ohio for mineral title to be split among multiple heirs from farmland passed down for generations, sometimes without clean probate. A title examiner can confirm your specific situation.

faqs.q: How long do Ohio Utica wells typically keep producing?
faqs.a: Many wells continue producing on their long, shallow tail for a decade or more after the initial decline, though the exact timeline depends on the well, formation, and how it's operated.

faqs.q: What documents does an Ohio buyer usually request?
faqs.a: Your division order, recent check stubs covering twelve to twenty-four months, and the deed or probate paperwork showing how you acquired the interest.

faqs.q: Can you sell only part of your Ohio interest?
faqs.a: Often yes. Many owners choose to sell a portion of a Utica interest while retaining the rest, which lets you take some value now while keeping exposure to future production.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Alaska
items.meta: Alaska mineral ownership works differently than the Lower 48. Here is who actually owns North Slope oil, what a private royalty check looks like, and how to sell.

sections.html:
Most of the ground under Prudhoe Bay and the North Slope belongs to the State of Alaska or Native corporations, not private individuals, so if you hold a private oil royalty here it is worth understanding exactly where it came from before you sell it.

Alaska is unusual among oil states because private mineral ownership is the exception rather than the rule. The State of Alaska owns most of the subsurface on the North Slope, Alaska Native regional and village corporations hold large blocks under the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, and only a smaller slice of interests sit in private hands, often tied to old homestead patents, native allotments, or fee mineral estates carved out before statehood-era land transfers were finalized.

If you are one of those private owners, your check is tied to production from fields like Prudhoe Bay, Kuparuk, Alpine, or one of the smaller satellite pools feeding the Trans-Alaska Pipeline. This page explains how that production behaves over time, why the North Slope's decline curve looks different from a shale play, and what to weigh before selling.

sections.title: Who Actually Owns Alaska Minerals
sections.html:
Before you assume your interest works like a typical Lower 48 royalty, it helps to confirm what kind of ownership you actually hold. Some Alaska residents receive dividend-style payments through a Native corporation, which is a different arrangement than a direct fee mineral or royalty interest tied to a specific lease and well. A true private royalty interest will show up as a numbered lease with a division order from the operator, the same as anywhere else.

Private fee interests on the North Slope typically trace back to land patented before large state and federal land transfers locked in current ownership. If your family has held an Alaska interest for decades, the original patent or deed on file with the state recorder's office is the starting point for confirming exactly what you own.

sections.title: How a North Slope Oil Check Moves
sections.html:
Prudhoe Bay has been producing since 1977, and like most giant conventional fields, its decline has been long and gradual rather than the steep early drop-off you see in a modern shale well. Total North Slope output has fallen from its 1980s peak, but individual legacy wells and their associated royalty interests have settled into a slower, more predictable slide, supplemented by newer satellite fields and infill drilling that keep the overall curve flatter than it would otherwise be.

That means an Alaska oil check is usually more about price than about a wild swing in barrels. Because Alaska crude typically prices off a different benchmark than Gulf Coast or Permian oil, your statement can move somewhat independently of what you read about national oil prices, so it is worth comparing your own recent history rather than assuming it tracks the headlines exactly.

sections.title: Distance, Logistics, and Why Records Matter More Here
sections.html:
Alaska's oil infrastructure is remote and capital-intensive, which means operators plan field life and maintenance further in advance than in a basin where a new well can be drilled in weeks. That longer planning horizon tends to produce steadier, more forecastable royalty payments once a field is established, since abrupt operational changes are less common than in a fast-drilling shale play.

It also means paperwork matters. Because so few Alaska interests are privately held, division orders and title records for the ones that are can be harder to track down than in a well-documented Texas or Oklahoma county. Confirming your interest through the state recorder and the operator's division order team before you sell saves time later.

sections.title: Deciding When to Sell an Alaska Interest
sections.html:
Because North Slope decline has historically been gradual, a private royalty owner is less likely to be staring down a cliff than an owner in a young shale play. That gives you more room to weigh a sale based on your own timeline, such as wanting a lump sum now instead of decades of smaller checks, rather than racing against a fast-falling curve.

Any offer on an Alaska interest gets built from your production history, the field's remaining life estimates, current oil pricing, and the strength of your title. the buyer walk you through that math before you decide anything.

faqs.q: Does every Alaskan own oil royalties?
faqs.a: No. Most North Slope subsurface belongs to the State of Alaska or Native corporations. A Permanent Fund dividend is not the same as a private oil royalty. A true private interest will show a specific lease and a division order from the operator.

faqs.q: Why is Alaska crude priced differently than what you see in the news?
faqs.a: North Slope oil typically settles against a different benchmark than West Texas Intermediate or Brent, so your check can move somewhat separately from headline oil prices. Comparing your own recent statements is more useful than comparing to national price news.

faqs.q: Is North Slope production declining fast?
faqs.a: Total North Slope output is well below its 1980s peak, but the decline has been gradual over decades rather than steep and sudden, helped by satellite fields and infill drilling. Individual legacy royalty interests tend to follow that same slow slide.

faqs.q: How do you confirm what you actually own in Alaska?
